A POST is retried only if its request carries exactly one idempotency key (from idempotency_key or header_params, header name matched case-insensitively): a bound header with no key behind it no longer enables retries; two different keys, or a blank key header, are refused rather than sent or dropped; a path parameter of . or .. is refused. submit_input refuses a key that is not 1 to 255 printable ASCII characters without surrounding whitespace and a case_id that is not one safe path segment, before any request is built.
from caliber.effects.connectors import classify_error, classify_result
from caliber.effects.connectors.document_request import CAPABILITY, submit_config, submit_input
from caliber.integrations.openapi.executor import OpenApiExecutionError, execute_openapi_http_tool

try:
    result = execute_openapi_http_tool(
        execution_config=submit_config(server_url),
        input_schema=None,
        input_data=submit_input(
            case_id=case_id, idempotency_key=proposal_key, expected_resource_version=7, body={"document_type": "pay_statement"}
        ),
    )
    outcome = classify_result(result, capability=CAPABILITY).outcome  # committed_receipt, definitive_rejection or ambiguous
except OpenApiExecutionError as error:
    outcome = classify_error(error).outcome  # proven_not_sent, or ambiguous: the effect may have happened
  • Not done here. The D1 report's other executor changes (a dedicated idempotency_key input in the derived tool schema, the expected version as a first-class input, an import that binds the key and retries, and a per-attempt log) are owned by #990, which must close before the D3 gate calls the connector decision met. The connector's submit_input puts the key and the version on the request itself, so the dispatcher does not depend on them. The dispatcher, receipts and the reconciler are B05.4 and B05.5.

Receipts: committed only with proof (B05.4a, #717)#

A 2xx answer from a downstream is a claim. caliber.effects.receipts (table caliber_effect_receipts, migration 0125) turns it into a receipt only after the platform has asked the downstream's own query and what came back is this proposal's effect.

  • What a receipt is checked against. ReceiptFacts (what the connector read back) must carry the proposal's logical key as the stored idempotency key, hash (as the intent rebuilt from the stored request) to the proposal's intent_hash, name the proposal's connector, connector version and target resource, and answer the dispatch attempt the proposal recorded. A mismatch is refused with the names of the fields that differ (ReceiptMismatch, code receipt_mismatch), never their values. The document-request connector's facts_from_lookup also requires, when the proposal expected a case version, that the stored version is exactly one more; a lookup that answers 404, a 5xx, a body that is not a stored request, another case or another document type gives no facts (and is not a failure).
  • Immutable, one per attempt, not borrowable. A receipt is the canonical receipt v1 record and its SHA-256, refused for update or delete by database triggers (and on PostgreSQL a CHECK ties the digest to the bytes); read_receipt recomputes the record from the columns and checks it against its proposal (key, intent, attempt, connector, target), so a row edited in place is receipt_corrupt (rewriting the columns and the bytes together would not be detected: there is no MAC, a limit of every immutable table here). The same facts delivered twice are one receipt (created=False; the response digest is not compared, because it hashes the whole lookup body, which can gain a field between deliveries, and the first one stays recorded); a different request id or resource version for the same attempt, or a downstream request id that already belongs to another proposal or attempt, are receipt_conflict and never replace the first. A receipt can be recorded while the proposal is dispatched, unknown or reconciled, not before it was dispatched and not after it settled (receipt_state).
  • committed needs a receipt, and failed cannot have one. transition(..., COMMITTED, receipt_id=...) verifies the receipt exists, was read back (query), and answers this proposal's attempt, key and intent (receipt_refused otherwise); the id is recorded on the proposal, and the database refuses a move to committed whose receipt_id is empty, does not exist or is another proposal's or attempt's. Once a verified receipt exists the proposal cannot be moved to failed (receipt_exists; the database refuses it too): failed is final, and the downstream's own query said it committed. The database also refuses a receipt for a proposal that is not dispatched, unknown or reconciled.
  • Settling a dispatch. settle_dispatch(session, proposal_id, outcome=..., verify=..., lease=...) first checks the proposal is still dispatched at expected_version, held by this owner and attempt, under this owner's lease (another owner or attempt is refused before a query is made and records nothing; whether the lease is still held is decided at the write, never before the query, so the lease row is not locked across the network call; a repeat of a settle that already happened is stale_version), then records what one attempt proved, the receipt and the commit as one unit (a refused commit keeps no receipt; if verify raises the proposal stays dispatched): a committed_receipt claim runs verify() (the authoritative query) and commits with the receipt if it confirms, and otherwise leaves the proposal unknown (receipt_unverified): a 404 or a mismatching stored request never certifies a failure, because a downstream that does not know a key yet may still process it; a definitive_rejection is failed (rejected:<code>), proven_not_sent is failed (not_sent) and ambiguous is unknown (ambiguous:<code>).
from caliber.effects.connectors.document_request import facts_from_lookup
from caliber.effects.receipts import settle_dispatch
from caliber.effects.records import proposal_state, proposal_view

view = proposal_view(session, proposal_id)

def verify():
    found = lookup_by_key(view.logical_key)  # the connector's query: {"status_code": ..., "json": ...}
    return facts_from_lookup(view, lookup_status=found["status_code"], lookup_body=found["json"])

settled = settle_dispatch(
    session,
    proposal_id,
    expected_version=proposal_state(session, proposal_id).version,
    owner_id=owner_id,
    attempt=attempt,
    lease=lease,  # the lease the owner captured; fenced in this transaction (B05.4a/B05.5a)
    outcome=outcome,  # from classify_result / classify_error
    verify=verify,
)
  • What this does and does not prove. record_receipt can only compare the facts it is handed with the proposal, so a receipt is as sound as the connector verifier that built them from the downstream's answer. For document-request, facts_from_lookup confirms the stored key, case, document type and (when the proposal expected a version) a stored version exactly one more, which holds only for a proposal built with document_request.build_intent: its arguments are exactly {"document_type": ...}, because that is all the downstream stores; a proposal with other arguments would commit downstream and then stay unknown. The proposal's effect class and expected version come from the proposal itself, so only the key, case, document type and version are checked against the downstream's data. Under REPEATABLE READ PostgreSQL refuses a competing insert as a serialization failure (store_failed): roll back and retry from a fresh read.
  • Not here. The dispatcher itself (B04.1). The reconciler for unknown and abandoned dispatched proposals is below.

Reconciler: only the owner asks about unknown and abandoned effects (B05.5b, #742)#

An effect with no recorded outcome is unknown, and an attempt whose dispatcher died or lost its lease while it was dispatched is abandoned: it may have been sent. Neither is ever dispatched again (there is no edge from unknown back to dispatched). caliber.effects.reconcile settles them the one way ADR 0003 allows: by asking the downstream by the original logical key, and believing only what it can prove.

  • Owner-only. reconcile_pass(factory, lease=..., targets=..., lookup=...) needs the Lease the execution owner captured, and every write re-compares it in the transaction that writes (fence_owner: exact owner and fencing token, database clock). No question is asked on a lease that is gone. A pass whose lease is taken over stops with ProposalError lease_lost; what it already settled stays settled and the new owner's pass takes the rest. Which process runs the pass, and when, belongs with the dispatcher's owner loop (B04.1); until then the pass is called by the code that holds the lease.
  • Abandoned means a prior lease. Migration 0126 records dispatch_token (the fencing token the owner held) with every dispatch. A dispatched proposal is abandoned exactly when its token is lower than the token of the lease the reconciler holds; abandon_dispatch then records unknown with reason abandoned_dispatch (under the reconciler's lease; not_abandoned for a dispatch under the current lease, which is in flight in this very process and is left alone, or one with no recorded token, which proves nothing). A dispatch under another token is also never a repeat of the dispatch before it.
  • Only authoritative terminal evidence moves it. The lookup runs outside any transaction, against the connector's own query, at the base_url of the CALIBER_EFFECT_CALLBACK_CONNECTORS binding for that connector and project (so it goes through the egress policy), and is read by the connector's capability record (interpret_lookup):
    The downstream saysRecordedOutcome
    a stored request that is this proposal's effect (key, intent, target, expected version)verified receipt, reconciled, committed; one audit entrycommitted
    404 from a connector that proves absence final (tombstone or honoured cancel, reads its own writes)reconciled, failed (absence_proven)failed
    404 from any other connector (document-request included): delayed visibility, or a request still in flightnothingunknown
    5xx, 401, an unreadable body, another request under the keynothingunknown / unverified
    cannot be reached, or no binding for this connector and projectnothinglookup_failed / not_bound

    A proposal that another actor moved while the downstream was asked is moved and is not overwritten (the write is conditioned on the version that was read).

  • Unknown blocks what depends on it. The runtime asks plan.effect_gate before every node, at the top of every attempt of its retries and before a guardrail re-runs the agents feeding it, with the node and everything it may depend on: every node upstream of it by edge, and the inline children of each of those (a for_each / loop / error_boundary target, a boundary's compensate_with, an agent's handoff targets), which have no edges of their own. While an effect any of them asked for is dispatched, unknown or reconciled, the node does not run and the run ends with UnknownEffectError: effect <proposal> (node <n>, unknown) has no final outcome: reconcile it ... (run status failed, error code runtime_error). The refusal is never absorbed: a fan-out item, a loop iteration, an error boundary or its compensation does not turn it into the item's own error. The queued-run worker installs the gate for every run.
  • A refused run is over; it is not resumed. The run is failed; once the reconciler settles the effect nothing restarts it. A new run is a new logical effect (the logical key includes the run id), so it is not gated by the old run's open effect and may ask the downstream for the same thing again: decide that with the operator before re-running something whose effect is unknown. Parking a gated run and resuming it after reconciliation is a follow-up.
from caliber.effects.callbacks import parse_bindings
from caliber.effects.reconcile import reconcile_pass, targets_from_bindings

targets = targets_from_bindings(parse_bindings(config.effect_callback_connectors))
for result in reconcile_pass(session_factory, lease=lease, targets=targets):
    print(result.proposal_id, result.outcome, result.state)  # committed | failed | unknown | unverified | lookup_failed | not_bound | in_flight | moved
  • Timeout example (V08). The connector's timeout fires after the request went out (ambiguous, recorded unknown with reason ambiguous:may_have_been_sent; not failed, the downstream may have committed, and not committed, nobody read a receipt). A retry from the node layer is refused (UnknownEffectError, the run ends failed), nothing can dispatch the proposal again (illegal_transition from unknown to dispatched), and the next reconciler pass finds the stored request by the original key and commits it with a verified receipt: one downstream mutation throughout (tests/egi_scenarios/test_v08_timeout_retry.py).
  • Refusals and recovery. lease_lost: you are no longer the owner, stop and let the new owner reconcile. store_failed: roll back and retry. unknown after a pass: nothing proves the outcome yet (delayed visibility looks like absence); the next pass asks again, the effect is never re-sent, and dependents stay blocked. There is no operator action that fails an unknown effect without the downstream's evidence yet (the operator view below lists them; an audited action is #997); a connector that can prove absence should set absence_proves_noncommit.
  • Limits. A pass looks at every candidate (a backlog that stays unknown cannot hide a newer one) and does not renew the lease: the caller bounds it with budget_seconds and renews or stops in on_progress. A dispatched row under the current lease is in_flight and is the dispatcher's to settle (it must record unknown on any error that is not a lost lease; the reconciler never abandons it). A dispatched row with no recorded token (none exist in shipped code; a downgrade through 0125 drops the column) is never abandoned. One connector (document-request) can be reconciled; another needs a verifier and capability record in reconcile.CONNECTORS. The gate runs where the runtime does (the queued-run worker, not preview or evaluation, which refuse effect nodes). A subworkflow's child plan is built separately and is not gated (the legacy effect ledger is not installed there either).

Operator reconciliation view: legacy claims and proposals, labelled apart (B05.6, #751)#

GET /caliber/system/effects (operator scope) lists two different records of an effect that may need a person, and never mixes them:

effects (source: legacy_ledger, source_version: ledger-v0)proposals (source: effect_proposal, source_version: proposal-v1)
What it isthe queued-run worker's claim ledger (caliber_effect_ledger)the ADR 0003 proposal ledger (caliber_effect_proposals)
Listed by defaultstatus=in_progress (status=any or another status widens it)the open states dispatched, unknown, reconciled (proposal_state=any or one state)
Settled byan operator: POST .../system/effects/{effect_key}/resolve (admin, audited: skip or retry)the reconciler's lookup by key; no operator action yet (safe_actions is empty)
safe_actionsresolve:skip, resolve:retry on an in_progress claim, none otherwisenone

Every row carries source, source_version and its own safe_actions, so a client cannot apply the legacy resolve to a proposal (it is refused, 400, and changes nothing) or read a proposal as a ledger claim. Legacy rows keep exactly the fields they always had (plus the label); the migrations that created the proposal tables leave them untouched and invent no receipt for them. A proposal row has identifiers, state, version, attempt, owner_id, dispatch_token, reason, receipt_id, timestamps, blocks_dependents (true while it is dispatched, unknown or reconciled: nothing that depends on it will run) and abandoned (for a dispatched attempt: true when a newer lease has replaced its dispatching lease and the reconciler will pick it up; false when no newer lease has been acquired, which is the dispatcher's own lease or one that lapsed with nobody to replace it yet; null for any other state, a row with no recorded token, or no lease at all). The proposal response therefore also carries lease (the stored execution-owner lease: owner_id, fencing_token, expires_at, expired, or null), so an operator can tell those two false cases apart. No row carries a payload: no arguments, intent bytes or recorded result (the query selects only the listed columns). The view is operator-scoped and system-wide: it shows every project's rows (each with its project_id, connector, resource and owner_id), like the rest of /system/*; reason is a short code by convention and must never carry a payload (recorders pass fixed codes). Known limit: no index on proposal state/created_at yet, so a very large ledger lists by scan (a follow-up if it grows). Query parameters: source (all by default, legacy or proposal), status, proposal_state, workflow_run_id, limit (1 to 1000, applied to each list; the proposal list reports proposals_truncated when more matched, newest first); proposal_state is only checked when proposals are asked for, and an unknown source or proposal_state is 400. The response also carries sources, a description of each kind (settled_by, safe_actions). SDK: client.system.effects(source="proposal", proposal_state="unknown").

Receipt callback: a connector tells the platform it is done (B05.4b, #725)#

POST /ajax-api/2.0/mlflow/caliber/effects/callbacks/receipt (caliber/src/caliber/routes/system_effects.py) lets a connector say "the effect for this idempotency key is done". It is not a CALIBER session (no identity, no CSRF token, no rate-limit bucket: the connector is the caller) and its only admission control is a signature. The body is exactly {"idempotency_key": "<key>"} and nothing else: the callback is a notification, and the platform asks the downstream itself (the connector's lookup by key) before it records anything.

  • Who may call. CALIBER_EFFECT_CALLBACK_CONNECTORS is a JSON array of bindings, each {connector, project_id, secret_source, base_url}: the connector, the one project it may act in, where its signing secret is read from (never the secret itself) and the base URL of its downstream. Empty (the default) accepts no callback; a malformed list stops the service at startup; the settings page shows only a count. One connector in one project has one secret; a connector bound to two projects has two. A secret shorter than 16 characters is refused (fail closed). The lookup the platform runs is the connector's plain GET by key (the binding has no authentication field yet, so it suits a downstream that allows it), goes through the egress policy (an internal downstream's host must be in CALIBER_EGRESS_ALLOWED_HOSTS) and is bounded: at most 4 lookups per connector and project at a time (503 busy, retryable).
  • The signature. Headers X-Caliber-Connector, X-Caliber-Project, X-Caliber-Timestamp (whole seconds, canonical: no leading zeros), X-Caliber-Delivery (an id unique per connector and project, 1 to 128 printable characters) and X-Caliber-Signature: v1=<hex>, the HMAC-SHA256 of v1\n<connector>\n<project>\n<timestamp>\n<delivery>\n<hex sha256 of the body> under the binding's secret. The connector, project, timestamp, delivery id and body are all inside the signed string, so a signature made for one connector, project or message is useless for another. A timestamp more than 300 seconds from the server's clock is refused; a captured message replayed inside the window can only make the platform ask the downstream again, and a receipt is recorded once.
  • One refusal. An unknown connector or project, a secret that cannot be read, a bad or malformed signature and a stale timestamp are all the same 401 {"detail": "callback rejected"}: a probe cannot tell them apart. After that, a body that is not exactly the key is 400, and a body over 4 KiB is 413.
  • Scope without leaks. The key is resolved to a proposal of this connector in this project; anything else (a key in another project, another connector's key, a key nobody has) is the same 404 {"detail": "no such proposal"}.
  • What happens. committed already: 200 already_committed. failed: 409 proposal_failed. Not yet dispatched: 409 not_dispatched. dispatched: 202 in_flight (the dispatcher, or the reconciler once the dispatch is abandoned, still owns it). unknown or reconciled: the platform runs the lookup outside any transaction. If the downstream cannot be asked: 502 lookup_failed. If it holds nothing under the key, or something that is not this proposal's effect: 202 unknown, the proposal stays unknown (a missing record is not a failure) and nothing is consumed. If it confirms, one transaction deduplicates the delivery (the inbox of B13.5a), records the verified receipt (B05.4a), moves unknown through reconciled to committed and audits it: 200 committed with the receipt_id.
  • Retryable, never half-consumed. The delivery id is consumed only together with the receipt and the commit; if any of it is refused (409 with the reason code, for example receipt_conflict or stale_version) the transaction rolls back and the same delivery can be sent again. The same delivery id with a different body is 409 inbox_payload_mismatch; the same delivery repeated after success is 200 duplicate (answered from the inbox before any query); a new delivery for an already committed proposal is 200 already_committed. Delivery ids are scoped to the binding (a digest of connector and project), so two projects' connectors never collide or burn each other's ids. A callback that loses a race to the commit is told already_committed, not a failure. Success bodies use the platform's {"data": ...} envelope.
import json
import time

from caliber.effects.callbacks import sign

body = json.dumps({"idempotency_key": proposal_key}).encode()
timestamp = int(time.time())
headers = {
    "X-Caliber-Connector": "document-request",
    "X-Caliber-Project": project_id,
    "X-Caliber-Timestamp": str(timestamp),
    "X-Caliber-Delivery": delivery_id,
    "X-Caliber-Signature": sign(secret, "document-request", project_id, timestamp, delivery_id, body),
}
  • Not here. The lease fencing of a dispatcher's own settle (B05.5a, above) does not apply to this callback, which is not an owner-only path; the callback commits an unknown or reconciled proposal only, never one a dispatcher still holds.

Approved context sources#

A run's context may only come from sources its project has approved (B07, #692). The inventory is caliber_approved_context_sources (caliber/src/caliber/context/sources.py): one row per (project, knowledge base, version), unique. approve_source(session, project_id, knowledge_base_id, version_id, actor) records an approval, revoke_source(...) withdraws it (the row stays, with revoked_at and revoked_by, as evidence) and is_approved(session, project_id, knowledge_base_id, version_id) answers whether it is approved now (False once revoked, for anything never approved and for a source that no longer exists). Admission reads it (B07.1b, #696): under CALIBER_PROFILE=reference every knowledge-base version a run can read must be approved for the run's project (require_approved, called by prepare_admission, so create-run, trigger, retry and the assistant tool all pass through it). That is the versions in the sealed bundle's dependency lock, the versions named on a knowledge-query node that names only version_ids, and the versions read by every child workflow the run calls (each child's own sealed bundle, which must be the one the parent was compiled against). A query whose version_ids arrive on an input port cannot be pinned, so it is refused outright. Otherwise the run is refused with 403, reason_code: source_not_approved in the error body and every unapproved knowledge_base_id@version_id named in the message, and nothing is stored. The role check (resource.execute on the project) comes first, so only a caller who may run the workflow learns what the project has approved. Approval and revocation take effect at the next admission: an idempotent retry of a request that was already admitted still returns that run, and a run already admitted keeps running on what it was pinned to (the load-time check is B07.2, #699). Not covered: cron-scheduler and service-token runs, which are not admitted in the first place (#958). A knowledge base that belongs to another project or to no project can never be approved for this one (only a project's own knowledge bases can), so a workflow pinned to one is refused until it uses one of the project's own. Development does not require approval. The refusal is not audited (it carries no policy decision); the response is the record.

  • A version, not a knowledge base. Approving version 1 approves nothing else; a new build must be approved on its own.
  • Only a project's own, real sources. The knowledge base must belong to the project and the version to that knowledge base. Every miss (unknown id, another project's knowledge base, a version of a different knowledge base) is one source_not_found refusal whose message names no identifier, so a foreign id cannot be probed.
  • Idempotent and race-safe. Approving an approved source returns the existing row; concurrent approvals create one (the unique key decides). Approving a revoked source reactivates the row with the new approver and time. Revoking a source that is not approved is not_approved. The row is read from the database and locked (FOR UPDATE on PostgreSQL) before it changes, so concurrent revocations or reactivations change and audit it once, and never overwrite who revoked it.
  • Completed builds of live knowledge bases only. The version must be completed (the rule that gates activating a version) and the knowledge base not archived; otherwise it is source_not_found. An approval whose version or knowledge base has since been deleted no longer counts (is_approved is false and approved_sources omits it); the row stays as evidence.
  • Audited. Approval and revocation each write an audit row (approve_context_source / revoke_context_source, entity context_source, ids only). The functions do not commit; they do not decide who may approve (the caller's project-role check does).
  • Not a foreign key to the knowledge base. The inventory outlives a deleted knowledge base on purpose; the loader must still check the version exists.

Authorizing a source before it is loaded (B07.2, #699)#

In the reference profile the run's own grant lists the context sources it may read: admission adds the action context.read and one resource per source, knowledge_base:<knowledge_base_id>@<version_id>, for exactly the sources it approved (the bundle's, its query nodes' and its child workflows'). When the worker builds an admitted run's plan it hands the knowledge-query runner a guard (caliber.context.authorize.source_guard_for), and the runner calls it with each version it is about to query, before the retrieval service is touched. The guard runs authorize_source(session, identity, run_manifest, grant_id, knowledge_base_id, version_id):

  1. the run's subject (derived from its stored manifest by identity_for_run) must equal the subject the manifest being checked recorded (identity_mismatch; a guard against mixing manifests, not a second authentication);
  2. the source must still be approved for the project (source_not_approved; a withdrawal after admission lands here and writes an audit row context_read_denied with ids only; no policy question is asked for a withdrawn source);
  3. decide(...) is asked with the manifest's run id, the exact grant id the manifest names, the manifest's typed subject and workload, context.read, the exact source resource and the manifest's purpose: a grant that does not list the source is resource_not_allowed, another run's grant grant_not_found, a member who left not_a_member, a revoked or expired grant is refused, and the decision (allow or deny) is recorded and audited like any other.

Every refusal is a ContextDenied with one fixed message that names no source (<code> (<reasons>): this run may not read that context source); the node fails and the run fails with the stable run error code context_denied (the code and the policy's reasons are in the summary), and nothing was loaded. An authority store that cannot answer is a refusal (authority_unavailable), and a database message is never put in the node's error text. context.read is a project action (owner, editor, reviewer) with policy risk 2. The guard is passed to child workflows the run calls.

run errormeaning and recovery
context_denied with source_not_approvedthe source was approved at admission and withdrawn since: approve it again, or resubmit the run on an approved version
context_denied with authority_denied (not_a_member) / grant_revoked / grant_expiredthe run's subject left the project, or its grant was revoked or ran out: resubmit as someone who may
context_denied with authority_denied (action_not_allowed) or (resource_not_allowed)the run's grant does not list that source (a run admitted before sources were authorized, or a query that reads a version the run was not admitted for): resubmit the run
context_denied with authority_unavailablethe authority store could not answer: nothing was loaded; resubmit when it is back

What it does not do. The guard follows how the run was admitted: it is built when the run's grant carries context.read (or this deployment requires approved sources), so a run admitted with sources stays guarded under any worker configuration. A run admitted before sources were authorized has no context.read and fails where sources are required (resubmit it). A grant holds at most 256 resources, so a run with 256 or more sources is refused at admission (grant_refused). The check is point-in-time: a withdrawal landing between the guard and the query does not stop that one read. Outputs a run already produced (replayed on a resume from a checkpoint) are not re-authorized. Each version queried costs one decision and one audit row (a query naming several versions authorizes each before any is read). Legacy runs have no guard. Not covered, tracked in #973: preview runs, evaluations, deploy gates, refinement and calibration, the assistant's knowledge tools, runtime export and knowledge_build nodes still read knowledge-base bytes without this check, and cron and service-token runs are not admitted (#958).

The context manifest#

What an agent step is given is recorded before the provider sees it (B07.3a, #704): caliber.context.manifest builds a context_manifest v1 record (ADR 0003) and stores it once in caliber_context_manifests, as canonical JSON with its SHA-256 (the record has no digest field: the digest excludes itself), unique per (run, step request, revision). Re-assembling a step is a new revision, never an edit; a revision that skips ahead or repeats is refused. UPDATE and DELETE are refused by database triggers and by the ORM (and, as for run manifests, run the application as a role without those privileges).

A manifest lists the segments in the order the provider sees them (position equals the index), each with (a segment's kind must match its source: a knowledge base's text can only be retrieved_text, an instruction can only come from a prompt):

  • a trust tier: instruction only for a system or workflow instruction (and every one is); everything else, the user's input, retrieved text, tool output, history and memory, is data. Text a source contains can never be promoted to an instruction by being retrieved;
  • its source (prompt, input, knowledge-base version, tool, memory, history), the retrieval and transform that produced it, and the digest of its content (the content is not stored in the manifest);
  • for payload loaded from a knowledge base or memory, the authorization decision id of the recorded context.read allow that let it be loaded: a segment without one is refused (unauthorized_payload), and storing the manifest checks each id against the recorded decision (an allow, of that action, for this run, of that exact source: knowledge_base:<kb>@<version> or memory:<reference>, decided no later than the manifest). A decision authorizes a read, not a step, so any step of its run may cite it;
  • the omitted and redacted items and the token allocation (budget, used, instruction, data; used is the sum of the segments and may not exceed the budget).

Storing also checks that the run exists and that the record's scope and project are the deployment's and the run's, and stores only canonical bytes. content_digest is a plain SHA-256 of the content, so a short, guessable value (a yes/no, an id) can be confirmed offline by anyone who can read the manifest: treat the record as evidence for the project's members and platform administrators, and do not expose it more widely without a keyed digest.

Reading a manifest back (read_context_manifest) re-checks the digest, the schema (an unknown schema_version is unknown_version, never read as the nearest) and every rule above, so a reordered or relabelled record is caught twice, by its digest and by its positions. Refusals carry a stable code: invalid_manifest, unknown_version, tier_violation, unauthorized_payload, ordering, tokens, authorization_rejected, duplicate_revision, revision_gap, rule_bundle_changed, rule_bundle_unavailable, rule_bundle_mismatch, rule_bundle_unpinned. Nothing here talks to a provider.

Recorded for every agent step (B07.3b, #710). For an admitted run in the reference profile the worker hands the runtime a recorder (caliber.context.assembly.context_recorder_for, built together with the source guard, or alone for a run whose manifest pins a rule bundle), and the runtime calls it with each agent step's initial context (the step's instructions as resolved when it is assembled, its skills, its history and the one input the provider is sent, with the node whose edge delivered it) before any of it reaches the provider, for every agent, every handoff target (a native Agents SDK handoff runs inside the provider call, so every agent the step may reach is recorded first) and in child workflows too. The recorder labels the assembly: the agent's own instructions are the only instruction tier; the history is one history data segment; text a knowledge query delivered straight to the agent is retrieved_text (one segment per version it read, citing the context.read decision the guard recorded when it authorized that version); the run's own input is user_input; any other text is tool_output of the node that delivered it, or of unknown origin (an item a for_each, loop or error_boundary hands an inline agent, text a knowledge query's output reached only through another node), which is still data and is never labelled the run's own input. It builds, validates and stores the manifest (its own short transaction, committed) as revision 1 of a fresh step request. If it cannot (an unknown or unauthorized source, a refused manifest, a database failure) the step does not run: the node fails (a for_each item or an error_boundary does not absorb the refusal), the run ends context_denied and the provider was never called. A document that says "ignore all previous instructions" is therefore recorded as data and reaches the agent as input, never as part of its instructions (scenario V03).

Caps and redaction (B07.4, #719). caliber.context.manifest.pack_context(segments, caps=..., redactor=...) is the one pure function that decides what an agent step's context may contain, and build_context_manifest records its result (omitted, redacted and sections=). It redacts every data-tier segment with the PII redactor (the same one the audit log uses, CALIBER_PII_REDACTION_*; an instruction is the operator's own text and is never altered) before the digest is taken, so the manifest hashes what the provider is given and the matched text is never recorded: a changed segment gets one redacted entry (fields: ["content"], reason: "redactor:pattern-1,pattern-3", naming which rules fired); a segment that is nothing but the replacement marker is dropped and listed in omitted as redacted. It caps the retrieved and history sections at the caps the caller passes (parse_section_caps(config.context_section_caps), from CALIBER_CONTEXT_SECTION_CAPS: JSON, default {"retrieved": 4000, "history": 2000}; only those two names are accepted and each cap is a positive integer, else the service refuses to start; a section left out is uncapped): chunks are kept in order while they fit, and the first chunk that does not fit and every later one in that section (they rank below it) is dropped and listed in omitted with reason token_budget and its tokens. The manifest's token_allocation.sections records each capped section's cap_tokens and used_tokens, and the manifest refuses a record where they do not add up to its segments. Example: with a cap of 10 and three retrieved chunks of 8 tokens, the manifest keeps the first chunk and lists two as token_budget; a chunk containing alice@example.com has its digest taken over the text with [REDACTED] in its place (the text itself is never stored). Not yet applied to a live step: the agent-step adapters (B08) call pack_context to decide what the provider receives. The recorder above (B07.3b) records the context as the runtime passes it and does not pack it, so until B08 consumes it no provider input is capped or redacted and the manifests it writes carry no sections; a manifest never claims a cap or a redaction that was not applied. The issue's draft names (allocation, redactions, budget) map onto the shipped v1 record (token_allocation.sections, redacted, token_budget), which is kept so manifests already written stay valid.

The rule bundle at context use (B07.5b, #736). A run admitted with a rule bundle has its path and SHA-256 in the run manifest (see "Admitting a run"); the run manifest is immutable and nothing here writes it. For every agent step the recorder reads the pin from that manifest, never from the current configuration, re-reads the bytes at the recorded path, re-hashes them on every step (nothing is trusted from an earlier step) and compares the hash with the recorded digest; only then are the bytes parsed (caliber.context.rules.rule_bundle_reference). The parse and the manifest entry are cached by the verified digest (a bounded LRU of 8 bundles): a digest is the hash of exactly one byte string, so a hit can only be the bundle those bytes parse to, and the cache never replaces the read and the hash. The step's context manifest then carries a rule_bundle entry: the bundle's bundle_id, version and sha256, and for each selected rule its rule_id, its source_ref (provenance) and the SHA-256 of its text (the rule text itself is not stored). Every rule of the operator-pinned bundle is selected, in bundle order. rule_bundle_reference also hands back the verified in-memory bundle (VerifiedRuleBundle.bundle): the B08 adapters must take rule text from that object and never reopen the path, so the text a provider is given is the text whose digest the manifest cites.

Storing the manifest checks the cited digest against the run manifest read from the database: a run admitted with a bundle cites it in every step, a run admitted without one cites none (a bundle enabled later is never applied to it, and no pin is backfilled). That store check is only the digest comparison; the rest of the entry (id, version, per-rule fields) is not re-derived there, because the store cannot re-read the file. The recorder, which verified the bytes the entry was built from, is the trust boundary for it.

A run that has a rule bundle is recorded even when it has no source guard (no approved sources required, no context.read grant); in that case no knowledge-base text is labelled retrieved_text (no source was authorized) and a query's text is tool_output of its node. Read tool_output there as "the output of this node", not as proof that the text did not come from a knowledge base: with no guard the platform did not authorize or label the source. So a path or configuration change after admission cannot alter what the run uses: the run uses the admitted bytes or is refused.

Size cap. A context manifest is bounded to 1 MiB and every step cites the bundle, so admission refuses a bundle whose citation (the canonical JSON of the entry above) exceeds 256 KiB (262144 bytes): rule_bundle_refused, with the size and the cap in the message and none of the file's content. A citation takes about 116 bytes per rule plus the UTF-8 length of its rule_id and source_ref (a CJK character is 3 bytes). Measured: 1000 rules with 100-character ASCII source refs take 217 KB (admitted); 150 rules with 512-character CJK source refs take 248 KB (admitted); 200 such rules take 331 KB and 1000 rules with 512-character ASCII source refs take 629 KB (both refused at admission, though the loader accepts the files). Shorten the source_ref values or split the bundle. A bundle admitted before this cap that is over it but under the manifest's 1 MiB bound keeps working; one over the bound fails every step with manifest_invalid.

run errormeaning and recovery
context_denied with rule_bundle_changedthe bytes at the pinned path are no longer the admitted bytes (an edit, even a comment or whitespace; a replaced file; a file larger than 1 MiB): the step did not run and no context manifest was written. The run stays failed: restoring the file does not revive it. Resubmit: the new run is admitted against the current CALIBER_RULE_BUNDLE_PATH and CALIBER_RULE_BUNDLE_SHA256, so after an intentional edit update both together first (a path with a stale digest is refused at admission)
context_denied with rule_bundle_unavailablethe pinned file is missing, not a regular file, unreadable, or the run manifest's pin is unusable. This includes a pinned path that existed when the run was admitted and is gone on the node that executes it (see "Which path is pinned"). The run stays failed; resubmit once the bundle is readable at the path a new admission will record
rule_bundle_refused at admission (409 manifest_refused)the configured bundle's bytes are missing, changed or invalid, or its citation is over the 256 KiB cap: fix the file or the pinned digest, or shorten the bundle; no run is created
context_denied with rule_bundle_mismatch / rule_bundle_unpinneda context manifest cited another bundle than the run's admitted one, or a bundle for a run admitted without one (the store refuses it; this indicates a defect, not an operator action)

Example. A run is admitted with CALIBER_RULE_BUNDLE_PATH=/etc/caliber/rules.yaml; an operator then appends a comment to the file. The worker's next agent step ends the run failed with error code context_denied and the summary rule_bundle_changed: the run's pinned rule bundle cannot be used now (digest_mismatch); the provider was never called and the run's manifest is untouched. Deleting the comment does not revive that run: it stays failed. Submitting the same request again creates a new run, admitted against whatever CALIBER_RULE_BUNDLE_PATH / CALIBER_RULE_BUNDLE_SHA256 say at that moment (the restored file with the old digest works; an intentionally edited file needs its new digest set together with the path). Changing those settings affects only runs admitted afterwards. The entry records provenance and digests, not the rule text: delivering rule text to the provider is the agent-step adapters' job (B08), as for caps and redaction, so a manifest never claims text was given that was not.

Which path is pinned. Admission records the symlink-resolved absolute path, and the worker that executes the run reads exactly that path. It must therefore exist, with the same bytes, on every node that can execute the run, for as long as the run can still take a step. Mounts that rotate their real directory break this: a Kubernetes ConfigMap or Secret volume serves rules.yaml -> ..data/rules.yaml where ..data points at a ..data_<timestamp> directory that is replaced and deleted on every update (and a Docker secret or a per-node temporary path differs between nodes). A run admitted before such a rotation records the old directory, which is gone, and its next step is refused as rule_bundle_unavailable. The run manifest's pin shape is immutable (#680, #726) and is not changed to work around this. Mount the bundle so its resolved path is stable and identical on every node.

Rollout. An in-place edit or rotation of the bundle file fails every in-flight or waiting run admitted against the old bytes at its next agent step. Use versioned, content-addressed file names (for example rules-<first 12 hex of the sha256>.yaml), publish the new file next to the old one, switch CALIBER_RULE_BUNDLE_PATH and CALIBER_RULE_BUNDLE_SHA256 together, and keep the old file in place until the runs admitted against it have drained (finished or failed).

Deploying the rule_bundle field. Adding rule_bundle to the context manifest is a readers-first change: an API pod or worker still running the previous release rejects a stored manifest that carries it (invalid_manifest, the v1 schema is closed). Roll the new release to every pod that reads context manifests before any worker running it can record one for a bundle-pinned run (or drain bundle-pinned runs first); do not mix releases while bundle-pinned runs are in flight.

What this does not cover, so it is not claimed: the tool specifications, the structured-output suffix and the results of tool calls made during a step are not in the manifest; a registry prompt is loaded when the step is assembled and again by the provider adapter, so an alias moved in between is not detected; session memory loaded for the step is recorded as history without a memory authorization (follow-up); a resumed run that replays a recorded knowledge-query output has no guard decision for it and is refused; a manifest is not linked to the NodeStep it describes, so a retried step adds a further revision-1 manifest; other model calls (a knowledge query's own answer synthesis, guardrail judges) are not agent steps and are not recorded. Token counts are an accounting estimate (four characters a token, and the recorded budget is the larger of the configured one and the total); enforcing a budget on a provider call is B08. Legacy runs and development have no recorder.

Approval requests: bound to the exact intent (B06.1, #706)#

A protected effect is approved by a person, and the approval has to say what it approves. create_approval_request (caliber/src/caliber/workflows/approval_requests.py) records a pending row in caliber_runtime_approval_requests that is bound to one effect proposal and to what the approver is shown (ADR 0003 approval_request; migration 0127). It runs in the caller's transaction and never commits. The route does not decide such a request yet (see "Not wired yet" below): this is the recorded question, not yet an answerable approval.

  • What is bound. proposal_id, the proposal's full intent_hash (sha256: and 64 hex digits, the digest every consumer reuses), its expected_resource_version (the downstream version the approval is valid for, or NULL), the evidence_hash of what the approver is shown, the policy_digest, requested_by and expires_at (now + ttl_seconds, UTC). The record is validated against approval_request.v1.json before the row is stored (risk_class is the proposal's effect class; every response is allowed: approve, reject, request_changes). Values are read from the stored proposal, never from the object the caller holds.
  • The node's own policy. The caller passes the node's ApprovalPolicy (required). It is stored as the request's policy_snapshot exactly as the decision route reads it back (ApprovalPolicy.from_snapshot), so a node that needs caliber.admin with a quorum of two, or a deployment that allows self-approval, is enforced as configured. policy_digest is computed (policy_digest(policy): sha256: and the SHA-256 of the canonical JSON of the snapshot) and cannot be supplied. It pins the policy as requested, not the approvers a quorum accumulates in the same snapshot afterwards. A policy the runtime cannot honour (unknown role, a count below 1, escalate or auto_reject, a non-boolean flag) is bad_field.
  • Only a proposed proposal. Any other state (already approved, dispatched, committed, failed, unknown or reconciled) raises ApprovalRequestError("proposal_not_proposed"), a ValueError whose message is that code; nothing is stored. A proposal that does not exist is proposal_not_found. A malformed evidence_hash (not sha256: and 64 lowercase hex digits), a requested_by that is blank, has leading or trailing whitespace, is over 256 characters or holds a control, zero-width or bidirectional character, a ttl_seconds that is not an integer from 1 to 31 536 000, or a now the expiry cannot be computed from (a date at the end of year 9999, not a datetime) is bad_field, and the message names the field. The one-year ceiling is a policy choice (a request open longer is a caller's mistake), not a configuration value or a storage limit.
  • Locking. The proposal row is read FOR UPDATE (a no-op on SQLite, whose write transaction is exclusive). Creators for one proposal serialize, and so do they against the proposal's own state transition: a proposal moving to approved either commits before the creator reads it (the creator refuses) or waits for the creator's transaction. Two creators for one proposed proposal both succeed, one after the other, and leave two pending rows: there is deliberately no unique index, and replacing the older request by the newer (superseded_by) is B06.2, which should take the same lock in the transaction that supersedes. The lock lasts until the caller commits or rolls back.
  • The binding is a database fact. A row is either legacy (every binding column NULL) or fully bound, never half-bound in either direction (ck_runtime_approval_bound); the three hash and digest columns are exactly 71 characters (ck_runtime_approval_digest_length); and a BEFORE UPDATE trigger (SQLite and PostgreSQL) refuses any change to proposal_id, intent_hash, evidence_hash, policy_digest, expected_resource_version, expires_at and requested_by: a request cannot be re-bound to another intent, nor a legacy row bound after the fact. status, the decision columns, policy_snapshot, superseded_by and consumed_at still move. PostgreSQL also enforces the proposal foreign key (SQLite does not enforce foreign keys in this repository).
  • Not wired yet. The decision routes refuse to decide a request that has a proposal_id: 409 with reason_code approval_bound_not_wired and a message that carries no id, hash or requester, for both approve and reject, and nothing is written. The default selection (no runtime_approval_id) ignores bound rows, so a legacy node-level request is never shadowed by a newer bound one. The list endpoint still shows bound rows. Until B06.2 (expiry and supersession) and B06.3 (recheck at commit) replace this refusal, an expired or superseded request is not refused either, because it cannot be decided at all. Known gaps for B06.3: the route's separation-of-duties check compares the approver with run.created_by, not with the bound requested_by; and it must also check that the proposal's run is still active before an approval is consumed.
  • Legacy rows stay valid. A node-level approval that guards no proposal keeps NULL in every new column and is decided exactly as before.
  • Migration. 0127 adds nine nullable columns, a foreign key, two checks, an index and the trigger (on PostgreSQL a function pinned to the schema); no backfill. Downgrade drops the trigger and function, the checks, the index and the columns; a legacy request is untouched and a bound one is lost. It needs 0126 (B05.5b) to be applied first.
  • Distinct actors. The separation-of-duties rule of record_approval is now assert_distinct_actor(actor, initiated_by, *, allow_self) (approval_policy.py): it raises ApprovalPolicyError ("the account that triggered this run cannot approve it; a second person must decide ...") when the actor is the initiator, unless allow_self (CALIBER_APPROVAL_ALLOW_SELF_APPROVAL) is set; an unknown initiator is not compared. actor_provenance.require_distinct_actors and the assistant service's author/reviewer checks are not delegated to it: they raise another error type, compare objects or other parties and have no allow_self, so sharing one function would change behaviour their callers pin.
from caliber.workflows.approval_policy import ApprovalPolicy
from caliber.workflows.approval_requests import ApprovalRequestError, create_approval_request

try:
    request = create_approval_request(
        session,
        proposal=proposal,
        policy=node_policy,  # the node's ApprovalPolicy; stored as the snapshot, digested into policy_digest
        evidence_hash=evidence_digest,  # "sha256:" + 64 hex digits
        requested_by="editor_a",
        ttl_seconds=86400,
    )
except ApprovalRequestError as refused:
    # refused.code is "proposal_not_proposed", "proposal_not_found" or "bad_field". For proposal_not_proposed the proposal has already
    # moved on: read its state, do not ask again for the same intent. Nothing was stored, so there is nothing to undo.
    ...
session.commit()  # the caller owns the transaction; the proposal row stays locked until then

Deciding such a request through the API today:

POST /ajax-api/2.0/mlflow/caliber/workflow-runs/{run_id}/approval/approve   {"runtime_approval_id": "<bound request>"}
409 {"detail": "this approval request is bound to an effect proposal and cannot be decided here yet: exact-intent approval is not wired",
     "status_code": 409, "reason_code": "approval_bound_not_wired"}

Agent steps: a request, a result, and no effects (B08.1a, #713)#

An agent step is one bounded unit of model work in a workflow node. Two control records (ADR 0003) describe it, and caliber.contracts.agent_step is the gate in front of both: it validates a record and refuses it before anything is dispatched. This page is the contract; the adapters that produce results (B08.1b onwards) and the limit and budget enforcement (B08.3, B08.4) build on it and are not part of it.

  • agent_step_request v1 names the step (step_request_id, workflow_run_id, node_id, the durable occurrence_id and the attempt), what it was given (run_manifest_digest and context_manifest_digest, each 64 lowercase hex digits), the one grant_id it runs under and its limits: max_turns, max_tool_calls, max_tokens (integers, zero allowed) and a deadline (RFC 3339 with an offset, ASCII digits, at most nine fractional digits, no leap second; StepLimits.deadline_at is the aware datetime, and nothing reads the clock). The platform enforces the limits, not the adapter. Every identifier is not blank and has no control character or lone surrogate, the rule the effect proposal applies.
  • The step and its id. The platform allocates one step_request_id for one (run, node, occurrence, attempt) tuple; the context manifest of the step carries the same id. A result must repeat the id and the tuple: one whose tuple matches but whose id differs, or whose id matches but whose tuple differs, is refused.
  • agent_step_result v1 answers it: the same five identifying fields, a stop_reason (completed, proposed_action, max_turns, max_tool_calls, max_tokens, deadline, refused, error), the provider's usage and at most one proposed_actions element, present exactly when the stop_reason is proposed_action. Optional: usage_source (provider when absent, estimated, unknown) and error_code (a short lowercase token, only with error or refused).
  • One proposed action per step, in v1. A logical effect is keyed by (run, node, occurrence), so a second action would share the first's key. The array stays so a later version can carry more, but only after it adds a per-action identity.
  • A step proposes; it never says anything happened. The result has no state, receipt or approval field and every schema is closed, so a result that claims a commit (state: committed, a receipt_id, stop_reason: committed) is refused like any other unknown field or value. An action becomes a recorded proposal only through caliber.effects.records, and committed there still needs a verified receipt.
  • What the model says is a claim, not a fact. Everything in a result is model output. In particular a proposed action's effect_class and connector_version are untrusted: a model can call an irreversible write read, and a read can be approved by policy alone. ProposedAction.bound_to(inventory_effect_class) returns the action carrying the platform's class (from the protected-effect inventory) and raises ClaimMismatch (code claim_mismatch) when the claim differs; B08.2 calls it before record_proposal, and an action that is not platform_bound is never recorded.
  • One action shape for the step and the proposal. A proposed action is effect_class (read, reversible_write, irreversible_write, export), target (connector and resource), connector_version, args and expected_resource_version: the names and meaning they have in the proposal record. ProposedAction.intent is the very caliber.effects.records.Intent of that proposal and ProposedAction.intent_hash its sha256: digest, so what a step proposed, what an approver is shown and what a receipt answers are one digest. An action is immutable (args is a read-only deep view; intent and record() are fresh copies, so nothing handed out can make the stored arguments disagree with the digest) and equal to another exactly when their canonical intents are ({"a": True} is not {"a": 1}). Parsing builds each intent, so args that are too deep (more than 64 levels), too large (the intent is at most 256 KiB) or not plain JSON are refused here too, not later at the store.
  • Usage and the token reservation. usage.total_tokens is what a budget settles against: it may not be less than prompt_tokens + completion_tokens, and cached_prompt_tokens may not exceed prompt_tokens. When a call failed or the provider gave no usage, report usage_source estimated or unknown rather than figures that look genuine. A refused or malformed result does not release the step's token reservation: B08.4 keeps a conservative charge for it.
  • Integers are integers. 1.0 is not an integer for these two kinds; attempt: 1.0 is refused, not coerced.
from caliber.contracts import ContractValidationError, UnsupportedSchemaVersion
from caliber.contracts.agent_step import parse_step_request, parse_step_result

request = parse_step_request(request_record)  # raises before any provider or tool is touched
try:
    result = parse_step_result(result_record, request)  # the request is required: a result is read as its answer
except UnsupportedSchemaVersion:
    ...  # a newer writer: refuse the step and upgrade this reader first, never read it as v1
except ContractValidationError as refusal:
    print(refusal.errors)  # the violations, by path and rule; nothing was dispatched
else:
    for action in result.proposed_actions:
        bound = action.bound_to(inventory_effect_class)  # the platform's class, or ClaimMismatch
        print(bound.intent_hash)  # submit as a proposal; the effect is still unperformed

Refusals are quiet. For these two kinds a refusal names the field and the rule, never the offending value, an unexpected property name or an unbounded amount of text: at most 20 violations are listed, an unsupported version is named only when it is a short plain token (else by its type), and a record of more than 1 MiB of JSON text (1048576 characters) is refused before it is validated. Other record kinds keep their messages. Refusals and what to do (ContractValidationError.errors, sorted by path):

the record hasrefused asrecover by
schema_version: "v2" (or anything but v1)UnsupportedSchemaVersion: agent_step_result schema_version v2 is not supported; supported: v1upgrading the reader before the writer (ADR 0003, readers before writers)
a field it does not define (state, receipt_id, a typo)<record>: additional properties are not allowed (proposed_actions/0: ... inside an action; the property is not named)removing the field; a step reports no state
stop_reason: "committed"stop_reason: is not one of ['completed', 'proposed_action', ...]reporting completed or proposed_action; a commit is the proposal's, with a receipt
effect_class: "write"proposed_actions/0/effect_class: is not one of ['read', 'reversible_write', 'irreversible_write', 'export']using one of the four classes of the connector inventory
an action with no targetproposed_actions/0: 'target' is a required propertynaming the connector and the resource
two or more actionsproposed_actions: violates maxItems 1proposing one effect per step; the next is the next occurrence
proposals with stop_reason: "completed", or proposed_action with noneproposed_actions: must equal [] or proposed_actions: violates minItems 1stopping with proposed_action exactly when there is a proposal
attempt: 1.0, a blank or control-character identifierattempt: must be of type integer, node_id: does not match the required patternintegers and printable identifiers
a total below the partsusage/total_tokens: is less than prompt_tokens + completion_tokensreporting the provider's total (or usage_source: "estimated")
a result for another stepstep_request_id: names another step than the request's, although run, node, occurrence and attempt are the same (or <field>: differs from the request's, although step_request_id is the same)applying only the result of the request that was asked
an action whose class the platform does not holdClaimMismatch: the step claimed effect_class 'read'; the platform's is 'irreversible_write'proposing nothing: the step's claim is discarded, the platform's class governs

A result that is refused is the end of that step's use of it: nothing was proposed, recorded or dispatched, and the retry is the same occurrence_id with the next attempt. A parse_* call is pure: it does not read the clock, so the deadline and the other limits are checked by the platform around the provider call (B08.3), not here.

Policy decisions#

caliber.policy.decisions.decide(...) (B03.3, #671; migration 0117, table caliber_policy_decisions) answers "may this run do this action on this resource, for this purpose, right now?" with a typed PolicyDecision and records it, allow or deny, immutably (ADR 0003 policy_decision v1 plus the run, subject and workload it was asked about; there are no foreign keys, so a decision about a grant that does not exist is still evidence).

  • Exact identity, no fallback. The caller supplies run_id, grant_id, the Subject and the Workload. A different run, an unknown grant, another subject (user, authentication method or project) and another workload each deny, and nothing is looked up by recency.
  • One reason, a fixed order: grant_not_found, subject_mismatch, workload_mismatch, grant_revoked, grant_expired, not_a_member, action_not_allowed, role_not_allowed, resource_not_allowed (the run grant checks, including the current membership and role), then the policy's own: policy_version_mismatch (the grant was issued under another policy version), purpose_not_allowed, explicit_deny, unknown_action_risk and risk_above_ceiling. An unavailable store is authority_unavailable. An allow carries no reason codes.
  • Explicit maps, never ordering. Each action has an explicit risk number in the policy (every action in resource_access.PROJECT_ACTIONS must have one; a test fails otherwise), compared with the policy's ceiling. policy-v1 has a ceiling of 4 (risk equal to the ceiling is allowed). Risk 5 means "a person, never a run": project administration (archive, restore, members, ownership transfer) and every approval or acceptance (resource.approve, release.approve, release.quality_signoff, change_request.accept), so no grant can make a run approve its own work (Beta keeps a human accountable owner and human protected-action approval, ADR 0004). Explicit denies are exact (action, resource) pairs. A Policy is read-only and type-checked.
  • Replayable. input_hash is the SHA-256 of the canonical JSON of every input (run, grant, subject, workload, action, resource, purpose and the live scopes) plus the policy's own digest; the clock is not an input. The same inputs under the same policy hash identically.
  • Transactions. A decision is flushed, never committed. For initial admission the run, its grant and the decision share one uncommitted transaction and the caller commits only after an allow; a denial rolls all of it back. If an decision cannot be recorded, the answer is a deny with persisted = False (an allow becomes authority_unavailable; a deny keeps its reason and gains authority_unavailable), and PolicyDecision.allowed is true only for a recorded allow. A decision never touches the run manifest. The record is written in a savepoint, so a failed record never poisons the caller's transaction. Consumers must know: a denied initial admission rolls its decision row back with the transaction, so evidence of a denial must be written separately (the audit record of B03.5, or a decision made in its own transaction), and on SQLite (development only) a savepoint that is the first write of a transaction commits it, so call decide after the run and grant writes.
  • Callers must not leak identity mismatches. decide records the specific reason (subject_mismatch and workload_mismatch reveal that a grant exists). It is server-internal: any layer that answers a client (HTTP, the admission API) must collapse identity and grant-lookup failures into one uniform refusal. purpose is stored verbatim: it names why, never context or payload.
  • Malformed input is a bug, not a decision. A blank, oversized or control-character id, action, resource or purpose, a naive now, or a non-Subject raises DecisionInputError and records nothing.
  • Immutable. Triggers refuse UPDATE and DELETE (TRUNCATE too on PostgreSQL) and the ORM raises ImmutableRecordError; as with run manifests, run the application as a role without those privileges.
  • Audited (B03.5, #688). Every recorded decision also writes one audit-log row through audit.record, in the decision's own savepoint, so the two exist together: action is policy_allow (severity standard) or policy_deny (severity high, or standard when every reason is ordinary lifecycle: grant_expired, grant_revoked, not_a_member), actor the subject, entity_type policy_decision, entity_id the decision id, and details the run, grant and workload ids, the action, resource and purpose, the result, the reason codes, the policy version and the input hash. The run's input, context and any secret are never in it (and the audit log's redactor runs over it anyway). If the decision and its audit row cannot be written (the store is down) the answer is an unrecorded deny (authority_unavailable) and one structured error log line carries the decision, run, grant, action and result; nothing is allowed that is not on record. At initial admission the decision's own rows are rolled back with the refused run (nothing about a refused run is stored), so the denial's audit row is written afterwards in its own short transaction from the decision's ids and reasons (admission.record_denial; a failure there is logged and never changes the refusal).

Recovery: grant_*, not_a_member, role_not_allowed, action_not_allowed and resource_not_allowed are as in the grant table above; policy_version_mismatch means the run must be admitted again under the current policy; purpose_not_allowed and explicit_deny are policy decisions to change deliberately, not retry; risk_above_ceiling means the action cannot be done by a run (use the human-approval path or a person); unknown_action_risk means the policy lacks a risk for the action and must be extended; subject_mismatch and workload_mismatch are always a bug or an attack: fix the caller.

Reserved tool names and refused paths (#641)#

The protected-effect inventory (docs/architecture/protected-effect-paths.md) classifies a built-in tool by its name, and the tool registry is unique only on (name, version). So a tool someone registers as grep_files could be taken for the built-in. Registration therefore refuses every name a built-in owns, and the inventory trusts a tool's name only when the tool really is CALIBER's own.

Reserved names. The sixteen tools CALIBER seeds: read_text_file, list_folder_files, grep_files, regex_search, grok_parse, sandbox_python, list_workdir_files, read_workdir_file, get_file_metadata, write_workdir_file, create_artifact, extract_document, memory_search, memory_list, list_entities and memory_add. The comparison is stricter than the resolver's exact match: case and surrounding spaces are ignored, and so are a tool. prefix and a .vN suffix, so Grep_Files, grep_files and tool.grep_files.v2 are all reserved. A name that merely contains one (grep_files_v2, my_grep_files) is free. The rule applies in every profile, to every owner, module and version.

Where it is enforced. POST /tools, POST /openapi-integrations/{id}/tool-drafts/{draft_id}/publish and the Aria publisher (AssistantPublisher, for a tool draft). Nothing is written when a name is refused. CALIBER's own seeding is unaffected.

POST /ajax-api/2.0/mlflow/caliber/tools   {"name": "grep_files", "version": "1.0", ...}
409 {"detail": "reserved_tool_name: tool name 'grep_files' is reserved for the built-in CALIBER tool
     'grep_files', which the protected-effect inventory classifies by name; register your tool under a
     different name", "status_code": 409}

The OpenAPI publish route answers the same 409; recover by publishing the draft again with another name in the request body. A tool draft Aria publishes under a reserved name is not registered: the draft ends as publish_failed and the publish report carries "success": false, "code": "reserved_tool_name" and the same message. Recover by asking Aria for a new tool draft under a different name and publishing that one.

A tool registered under a built-in's name before this rule is not migrated or rewritten. It is neutralised by two things only: the identity check and an audit. A registry row counts as CALIBER's own only when every field the seed writes matches (workflows.builtin_tools.is_builtin_tool): the name, the owner @caliber, the version 1.0, a callable named like the tool, and that tool's own module (BUILTIN_TOOL_MODULE_BY_NAME, which the seed also reads, so the two cannot drift). effects.inventory.effect_class_for_registry_tool classifies every other row as irreversible_write, the fail-closed class, and tool_disposition_for_registry_tool routes it through the dispatcher instead of trusting it. The audit: every time the tool list seeds the built-ins, each row that holds a reserved name without being the seed's own row is logged once per process at ERROR and gets one audit record (action flag_reserved_tool_name, entity type tool, severity high, with blocks_seed). blocks_seed: true means the row is at version 1.0 under the exact built-in name, so the registry (unique on name and version) cannot hold the real built-in: it was never seeded and is missing from the list until the squatter is archived and renamed, or deleted by an operator. To rename such a tool, register it again under a new name, point the workflows that use it at the new name, then archive the old one (a registered tool cannot be renamed in place).

The owner is part of that identity, so PATCH /tools/{id} refuses (409 reserved_tool_owner) to give a registered tool the owner @caliber, unless the row already matches the seed in every other field. That exception exists to repair a built-in whose owner was edited away: until it is set back the row is untrusted (fail-closed) and the audit flags it; a row that differs from the seed in name, version, module or callable can never be made trusted by editing its owner.

Where trust comes from at run time. The dispatch call sites (B07 #524, B08 #526, the B04 tasks) must pass the registry row's own name, owner, module, callable and version, read from the database for the tool being run. They must never pass a manifest binding's local_name or resolved_name, and IRToolBinding and ToolRegistryEntry carry no owner on purpose: the IR is written into generated exports field by field, so an owner there would be data an export author controls. A test fails when production code passes a constant or a **kwargs expansion to these lookups.

Refused until explicitly supported. The inventory now marks two paths refuse for the reference profile, so the dispatcher (B04.7, #774) will refuse them with unsupported_in_reference_profile:

inventory rowpathwhy
EP-055the host-file tools read_text_file, list_folder_files, grep_files, regex_searchthey read any host path, with no confine_to_file_root, and return what they read to the model provider (an export)
EP-114the write tools of the first-party PostgreSQL MCP server (create_table, insert_rows, update_rows, delete_rows, execute_sql, create_vector_table, upsert_vectors, create_graph, drop_graph, create_vertex, create_edge, cypher_query)they create tables and write rows with no guard of their own; its read tools (list_tables, describe_table, run_query, similarity_search) run in a read-only transaction and are not refused

effects.inventory.tool_disposition(name, caliber_defined=...) answers refuse or dispatch for a tool, on the same trust rule as effect_class. The DB MCP write tools are not registry rows, so tool_disposition_for_registry_tool answers dispatch for those names today; their refusal rests on the MCP server's identity, which #759 and #774 establish. This change records the decision and the lookup; the dispatcher that raises the refusal at run time is #774. Until it lands a reference deployment still runs these tools if a workflow uses them, so do not register the first-party DB MCP server and do not wire the four host-file tools into a reference workflow.

Configuration, migration and rollback. No new setting, no migration and no stored data change. Rolling back is reverting the change; rows already refused were never written.

Not enforced yet#

ADR 0001 describes the whole reference shape; this table is what the process checks today. Not checked:

  • The shape itself: one tenant and region, MLflow addressed by MLFLOW_TRACKING_URI, an S3-compatible object store, at least two projects, and one real model provider next to the scripted adapter. Readiness reporting for MLflow and the object store is #535. The PostgreSQL version and the pgvector extension are checked by the migrations (migration 0060) and the migration-parity CI job, not by the profile.
  • Origin rules (#533). ADR 0001 names them, but #533 has no allowed-origins task yet; that rule is not scheduled.
  • Run-time refusal of the refuse inventory rows, including the host-file tools and the DB MCP write tools (#774; see "Reserved tool names and refused paths"), the trusted-connector set (#534), the full attack pack (#535), a single execution owner (#536) and the Apply separation-of-duties flag (#589).
  • Cookie flags: auth_session_cookie_secure is not checked.
  • The database role: whether the application connects as a role without UPDATE, DELETE or TRUNCATE on caliber_run_manifests (see "Run manifests are written once").

A configuration that passes this page is the minimum for the reference profile, not the whole of it.
